query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory BCC high‐entropy alloys, a dominant population of edge dislocations creates higher lattice friction that impedes dislocation motion, thereby governing and enhancing hardness and strength even at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, refractory BCC high‐entropy alloy (e.g. an NbTaTiV‐based HEA) in its as-processed (undeformed) state.
generation.intervention: Process one set of samples to promote edge dislocation activity (via controlled deformation parameters known to favor edge dislocation multiplication) and compare them against a control alloy—either a conventional BCC metal or a HEA known to be screw dislocation–dominated.
generation.conditions: Both the intervention and control samples are subjected to identical mechanical testing (nanoindentation and tensile tests) at room temperature and over an elevated temperature range up to approximately 1073 K, under standardized strain rates and environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The relative fraction of edge versus screw dislocations in the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: A higher density of mobile edge dislocations increases the lattice friction and acts as effective barriers to plastic flow, which raises the hardness and yield strength of the refractory HEA. This mechanism is expected to be less sensitive to temperature, resulting in a strength plateau at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline control (a conventional BCC alloy or HEA with predominantly screw dislocations), the refractory HEA exhibiting edge dislocation dominance will show increased hardness and yield strength, along with a notable retention of strength (e.g. a plateau behavior) in the temperature range up to ~1073 K.
generation.baseline: Conventional BCC alloys or HEAs where plasticity is primarily governed by screw dislocation mobility.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for refractory BCC high‐entropy alloys with similar chemical complexity under standard mechanical test conditions (nanoindentation and tensile testing) and primarily within the temperature range from room temperature to approximately 1073 K.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative enhancement in hardness and strength may vary with the exact alloy composition, processing history, and testing conditions. The precise percentage increase or the critical temperature limits require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: (A) a refractory BCC HEA (e.g. NbTaTiV composition) processed under conditions intended to maximize edge dislocation density; (B) a control alloy (a conventional BCC alloy or a HEA where screw dislocations dominate). Subject both groups to identical nanoindentation and tensile testing at room temperature and across an elevated temperature range (up to ~1073 K). Additionally, use high-resolution TEM to quantify dislocation types in each specimen.
measurements: Yield strength from tensile tests over the temperature range
Dislocation character and density via TEM imaging (ratio of edge to screw dislocations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refractory HEA with intended edge dislocation dominance does not display a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength, or if no relative predominance of edge dislocations is observed compared to the control, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations. We use the insight and theory to perform a computationally-guided search over 107 BCC HEAs and identify over 106 possible ultra-strong high-T alloy compositions for future exploration.Subject terms: Mechanical engineering, Mechanical properties, Computational methods The strength in BCC high-entropy alloys is associated with the type of mobile dislocations.
